cards.b: Capital: spending on non-current assets lasting over a year (machinery). Revenue: day-to-day expenses (wages, rent, materials).
Retained profit, sale of existing assets, owner's savings.
No interest or repayment and no loss of control, but not available to new or loss-making businesses.
Long-term finance only for limited companies. No interest or repayment, but shareholders expect dividends and control may be diluted.
Medium to long-term, repaid with interest over a set period. Needs security (collateral); owners keep control.
Short-term: bank lets the business withdraw more than it has, up to a limit. Flexible but high interest and repayable on demand.
Suppliers let the business pay later (30–60 days). No interest, but discounts for early payment may be lost.
Selling trade receivables to a debt factor for immediate cash. The business receives less than the full amount.
Hire purchase: deposit plus instalments, then the business owns the asset. Leasing: renting an asset, never owned.
Microfinance: very small loans to people who cannot get bank loans. Crowdfunding: many people each invest a small amount, usually online.
Long-term assets (factory) need long-term finance (loan, shares). Short-term needs (wages) use overdraft or trade credit.
Business plan, cash-flow forecast, collateral, existing debts, owner's experience and own investment.
A profitable business can run out of cash if customers pay late or money is tied up in inventory or assets.
Net cash flow = inflows − outflows. Closing balance = opening balance + net cash flow. Next month's opening = this closing.
Current assets − current liabilities. Finance to pay day-to-day expenses. Too little means debts cannot be paid.

short.q: Explain why a profitable business might run out of cash. [3]
short.model: Customers may pay late on credit, or cash may be spent on inventory or equipment. The business then cannot pay wages or suppliers even though it is profitable.
points: credit sales not yet paid / cash spent on assets

short.q: Calculate the closing balance when opening balance is €1,000, inflows €12,000 and outflows €9,500. [2]
Explain why an overdraft is not suitable for buying a new factory. [3]
short.model: An overdraft is short-term and repayable on demand with high interest. A factory is a long-term asset, so long-term finance such as a loan or shares is better.

short.q: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of leasing a machine rather than buying it. [4]
short.model: Advantage: no large outlay, which protects cash flow. Disadvantage: the business never owns the asset and total cost is higher.

short.q: Explain two ways a business could improve a short-term cash-flow problem. [4]
short.model: It could ask customers to pay sooner, which brings cash in faster. It could delay buying equipment, which reduces outflows.
